title: Empire, Exams and Neo-Confucianism
bigQuestion: How did the classics shape who held power in imperial China and East Asia, and who was left out?

story.title: The Last Exam
story.kicker: In 1905 an imperial order ends an exam system that had shaped China for thirteen centuries.
paragraphs: September 1905. In the Qing capital, Beijing, officials read an imperial edict. Beginning at once, it says, the civil-service examinations will stop. The country will build modern schools instead. The order is short. Its effect is enormous.

Across China, hundreds of thousands of men had been studying for the next round. Some were teenagers. Some were grandfathers who had taken the exams again and again. Their years of memorizing the Four Books and Five Classics would no longer lead to office.

For thirteen centuries, since about 605 CE, the exams had been the main road to government service. They had carried Zhu Xi's reading of the classics into every village school. They had made a scholar-official class that ruled China, and inspired similar exams in Korea and Vietnam.

Reformers cheered the change. China, they said, needed science, engineering and law to face foreign powers. Others grieved a world that was ending. The classics did not vanish, but they lost the place they had held at the center of Chinese life.
story.think: Why might one change to an exam system change a whole society?

lessons.title: Han State Confucianism
lessons.mainIdea: The Han dynasty used Confucian learning to train officials and to explain the emperor's role, while keeping strict laws.
reading: The Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE) gave Confucian learning official support. Officials were expected to know the Five Classics. The scholar Dong Zhongshu described the emperor as a link between Heaven, Earth and humanity. Disasters, he taught, could be signs from Heaven that a ruler was going wrong.

The Han also made *filial piety*, respect and care for parents, a public value. Officials were sometimes recommended for office because of their devotion to parents. The short Classic of Filial Piety became widely taught.

Historians describe this as *state Confucianism*: the government using Confucian ideas to support its rule. Some Confucians welcomed it. Others worried that serving the state could bend the teaching. Han law still owed much to Legalism.

words.d: the government's use of Confucian learning to train officials and support its rule
xiao; respect and care for parents, a key Confucian value
a Han scholar who linked Confucian teaching to the emperor's role under Heaven

look.title: Heaven's Warning
look.text: An earthquake shakes the capital. An official writes to the emperor: 'Heaven is warning Your Majesty. Lower the taxes, pardon prisoners and seek honest advisers.' The emperor issues an order to do so.
look.prompt: How does Dong Zhongshu's idea give officials a way to criticize the emperor? What are its limits?

check.q: What is state Confucianism?
choices: The government using Confucian learning to support its rule
check.why: Historians use the term for the Han state's official use of Confucian learning.

check.q: What did Dong Zhongshu teach about disasters?
choices: They show the Legalists were right
They could be Heaven's warnings to a ruler
check.why: Dong Zhongshu taught that disasters might be Heaven's signs to a ruler going wrong.

check.q: Which value did the Han promote publicly?
check.why: The Han promoted xiao, filial piety, even in choosing officials.

lessons.title: Buddhism Arrives
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhism came to China from India along trade routes by the first century CE and became one of the 'three teachings' with Confucianism and Daoism.
reading: *Buddhism* began in India with the Buddha, around the 400s BCE. Monks and merchants carried it to China along the Silk Roads. Chinese tradition dates its arrival to the first century CE and links it to the White Horse Temple near Luoyang.

At first, translators used Daoist words to explain Buddhist ideas. Over time Buddhism grew into a major Chinese religion, with monasteries, schools of thought such as Chan (Zen), and millions of followers. Some Confucians criticized it, since monks left their families.

By the Tang dynasty (618–907), people often spoke of the *three teachings*: Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism. Emperors sometimes favored one over another. Many ordinary people drew on all three. A popular saying held that the three teachings are one.

words.d: a tradition founded by the Buddha in India, which spread to China by the first century CE
Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism, often seen side by side in China
a Chinese school of Buddhism focused on meditation; called Zen in Japan

check.q: Where did Buddhism begin?
check.why: Buddhism began in India with the Buddha and reached China by trade routes.

check.q: Why did some Confucians criticize Buddhism?
check.why: Confucians valued family duty and criticized monks for leaving home.

lessons.title: How the Exams Worked
lessons.mainIdea: From the Sui and Tang to 1905, the civil-service exams tested knowledge of the classics in several levels, from local to palace.
reading: The Sui dynasty began exams for officials around 605 CE. The Tang used them, and the Song (960–1279) expanded them greatly. Printing made books cheaper, so more families could prepare. Exams became the main road to office.

By the Ming and Qing, there were several *levels*. Candidates passed local exams, then provincial exams held every three years, then the metropolitan exam in the capital. The best faced a *palace exam* before the emperor. Few reached the top degree, the jinshi.

Candidates sat in tiny cells for days. Graders copied essays so handwriting could not reveal names, to prevent favoritism. Cheating still happened. Some candidates wore undershirts covered with tiny copied classics, which museums preserve today.

words.d: the highest degree in the imperial exams, earned at the capital
the final exam, held before the emperor, for the top candidates
a man who passed the exams and served in government

look.title: A Cell for Three Days
look.text: Picture a row of hundreds of tiny brick cells, each open on one side. Inside, a board for a desk and a board for a seat. A candidate brings food, ink, brushes and a blanket. He stays for about three days, writing essays on passages from the Four Books.
look.prompt: What do the conditions tell you about how much the exams mattered? What skills besides knowledge would a candidate need?

check.q: Which dynasty began the exams, around 605 CE?
check.why: The Sui dynasty started the exams around 605 CE.

check.q: Why were essays copied before grading?
choices: To prevent favoritism by hiding handwriting
check.why: Copying hid candidates' identity so graders could not favor anyone.

check.q: What was the jinshi?
check.why: The jinshi was the top degree, earned at the capital.

lessons.title: Zhu Xi Becomes the Standard
lessons.mainIdea: In 1313 Zhu Xi's commentaries on the Four Books became the exam standard, spreading Neo-Confucian readings across China.
reading: *Neo-Confucianism* is a modern name for the renewed Confucian thought of the Song and later dynasties. Its thinkers answered Buddhism and Daoism with their own big picture of the universe. Zhu Xi (1130–1200) was its greatest systematizer.

Zhu Xi taught that everything has *li*, principle, the pattern that makes it what it is, and *qi*, the stuff or energy of which it is made. Human nature is principle and is good, he said, as Mencius taught, but cloudy qi can hide it. Study of things and self-cultivation clear it.

In 1313, the Yuan government made Zhu Xi's commentaries the exam standard. This lasted to 1905. Later, Wang Yangming (1472–1529) challenged Zhu Xi, teaching that principle is found in one's own mind and that knowing and acting are one.

words.d: renewed Confucian thought from the Song dynasty on, led by thinkers like Zhu Xi
in Zhu Xi's thought, the pattern that makes each thing what it is
in Zhu Xi's thought, the energy or stuff of which things are made
Ming thinker (1472–1529) who taught the unity of knowing and acting

look.title: Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming
look.text: Zhu Xi: 'To understand principle, investigate things one by one, read the classics carefully, and your understanding will one day open up.' Wang Yangming: 'Principle is in your own mind. To know the good truly is already to act on it.'
look.prompt: How would each thinker advise a student who wants to become good? Describe both without choosing.

check.q: In Zhu Xi's thought, what is li (principle)?
choices: The pattern that makes each thing what it is
check.why: Zhu Xi's li is the principle or pattern in each thing.

check.q: What did Wang Yangming teach?
check.why: Wang Yangming taught the unity of knowledge and action.

check.q: Which ancient thinker did Zhu Xi follow on human nature?
check.why: Zhu Xi held, like Mencius, that human nature is good.

lessons.title: Who Was Left Out
lessons.mainIdea: The exams claimed to reward merit, but women and several groups were barred, and few poor families could afford years of study.
reading: Confucius taught, in Analects 15.38 (15.39 in some editions), that in teaching there should be no distinction of classes. The exams were praised as open to talent. In practice, many people could not take them.

Women were barred from the exams for their whole history. Sons of some groups, such as actors and certain hereditary servants, were also excluded. Poor farm families rarely could spare a son for years of study or pay a teacher. Most passing candidates came from families with land or learning.

Historians still debate how much the exams allowed *social mobility*, the chance to rise from one's birth. Some studies find a real share of degree-holders had no recent ancestors with degrees. Others stress how *exclusion* limited the system.

words.d: the chance to move up or down in society from the position one was born into
keeping certain people out
ability and achievement, rather than family or wealth

check.why: Women could not sit for the imperial exams.

check.why: Legge's 15.38: 'In teaching there should be no distinction of classes.'

lessons.title: Ban Zhao's Lessons for Women
lessons.mainIdea: Ban Zhao, a Han scholar, wrote Lessons for Women (c. 100 CE), which taught humility and duty and also argued that girls should be educated.
reading: *Ban Zhao* (c. 45–c. 117 CE) was one of the most learned people of the Han. She helped finish the History of the Former Han that her brother Ban Gu had begun, and she taught at the imperial court.

Around 100 CE she wrote *Lessons for Women* (Nüjie), advice for the young women of her family. It teaches humility, hard work and obedience to husbands and in-laws, following the Confucian idea of the five relationships. It became a standard text for girls for centuries.

Readers have taken it in different ways. Many modern critics see it as teaching women to accept a lower place. Others note that Ban Zhao argued girls, like boys, should be taught to read, and that her own life showed a woman as a scholar. Historians read it in its Han context.

words.d: a Han scholar and historian (c. 45–c. 117 CE) who wrote Lessons for Women
Nüjie, Ban Zhao's advice text for women, c. 100 CE
ruler–subject, father–son, husband–wife, elder–younger brother and friend–friend

look.title: Educate Girls Too
look.text: Ban Zhao notes that boys are taught to read at eight and study until fifteen. She asks why girls should not be taught the same way, so they can understand their duties.
look.cite: Ban Zhao, Lessons for Women (c. 100 CE), ch. 2, paraphrased; see Nancy Lee Swann, Pan Chao (1932)
look.prompt: How does this passage complicate the view of Lessons for Women as only about obedience?

check.q: Who was Ban Zhao?
check.why: Ban Zhao was a leading Han scholar who helped finish the History of the Former Han.

check.q: What did Ban Zhao argue about girls?
choices: They should be taught to read, like boys
check.why: In Lessons for Women she argues girls should be educated as boys are.

check.q: How do many modern critics read Lessons for Women?
choices: As teaching women to accept a lower place
check.why: Many critics see its teaching of obedience as limiting women; others stress its context and its call for education.

lessons.title: Korea, Japan and Vietnam
lessons.mainIdea: Neo-Confucian learning shaped government and education in Joseon Korea, Tokugawa Japan and Vietnam, each in its own way.
reading: In Korea, the *Joseon* dynasty (1392–1910) made Neo-Confucianism its guiding philosophy. The national academy, Seonggyungwan, trained scholars. Thinkers such as Yi Hwang (Toegye) and Yi I (Yulgok) debated Zhu Xi's ideas of principle and qi in depth. Ancestral rites spread widely.

In Japan, the Tokugawa shoguns (1603–1868) supported Confucian scholars such as Hayashi Razan. Japan did not use exams to choose officials, since rank was mostly hereditary. Still, Confucian ideas shaped schools and samurai ethics.

In Vietnam, the *Temple of Literature* in Hanoi, founded in 1070, honors Confucius. Stone tablets on the backs of stone turtles list doctoral laureates from the 1400s onward. Vietnam held classical exams until 1919.

words.d: a Korean dynasty (1392–1910) that made Neo-Confucianism official
a temple to Confucius in Hanoi, founded 1070, with stone tablets of exam laureates
the shoguns who ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868

lessons.title: Critics and Revivals
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1900s, Chinese reformers attacked Confucianism, a 1970s campaign targeted Confucius, and later decades saw a revival of interest.
reading: After 1905, many young reformers blamed Confucian tradition for China's weakness. In the May Fourth Movement of 1919, writers such as Lu Xun criticized family rules and the treatment of women. A popular slogan called for overthrowing the "Confucian shop."

Under Mao Zedong, the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976) attacked old traditions. In 1973–74, a political campaign called "Criticize Lin Biao, Criticize Confucius" denounced Confucius. Red Guards damaged temples and tombs, including at Qufu, in 1966.

Since the 1980s, interest has returned. The Qufu temple was restored. Scholars in China, Taiwan, Korea and the West study "New Confucianism." Some welcome the *revival*; others worry that governments use it to promote obedience. The debate continues.

words.d: a 1919 movement of Chinese students and writers calling for science, democracy and new culture
a 1966–1976 political campaign in China that attacked old traditions
a return of interest in something after a time of decline
